english_translation: Shine your light because it is very dark where you are; I cannot see anything.

dialogue.shona: Vhenekera mwenje wako nokuti kwamuri kwakasviba zvikuru; hapana chandiri kuona.
dialogue.english: Shine your light because it is very dark where you are; I cannot see anything.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Vhenekera [vhenekera] • mwenje [mwenje] • wako [wako] • nokuti [because] • kwamuri [kwamuri] • kwakasviba [kwakasviba] • zvikuru [very much / greatly] • hapana [hapana] • chandiri [chandiri] • kuona [to / at ona]

grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Vhenekera')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'Vhenekera' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). When speaking to more than one person, or when showing polite respect to an adult, you add '-i' to the end, changing '-a' to '-ai' (as in 'Huyai!' = 'Come!' or 'Batai!' = 'Catch/Hold!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.
grammar_notes.rule: Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('wako')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'wako' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

grammar_notes.title: Describing How Actions Are Done: Adverbs & Intensifiers ('zvikuru')
grammar_notes.content: To describe HOW an action is performed, Shona frequently uses the prefix 'zva-' / 'zvi-' or intensifiers like 'zvikuru'. Compare these high-frequency expressions you will hear every day: 'zvakanaka' ('well / nicely'), 'zvakasimba' ('firmly / strongly'), 'zvishoma' ('a little bit'), 'zvinyoronyoro' ('gently / softly'), and 'chaizvo' or 'zvikuru' ('very much / davvero').
grammar_notes.rule: Verb + Adverb of Manner/Degree (zvakanaka = well, zvakasimba = firmly, zvishoma = a little, chaizvo/zvikuru = very much)

cultural_notes.title: Torches, Lanterns ('Mwenje') & Walking Safely After Dark
cultural_notes.content: Out in the countryside where there are no streetlights—or during an evening power outage—carrying a bright torch or solar lantern ('kuvhenekera mwenje') lights the footpath safely under the starry southern sky.
